definition: Lasting for a very short time
exampleSentence: The ephemeral beauty of cherry blossoms makes them all the more special.

definition: Present, appearing, or found everywhere
exampleSentence: Smartphones have become ubiquitous in modern society.
etymology: From Latin 'ubique' (everywhere), from 'ubi' (where). Related to the same root as 'alibi' — both are about location.

definition: The occurrence of fortunate events by chance
exampleSentence: Meeting my best friend on that train was pure serendipity.

definition: A feeling of pensive sadness, typically with no obvious cause
exampleSentence: A sense of melancholy settled over him as autumn arrived.

definition: Able to recover quickly from difficulties; tough
exampleSentence: Children are often more resilient than adults give them credit for.

definition: Fluent or persuasive in speaking or writing
exampleSentence: She delivered an eloquent speech that moved the entire audience.

definition: Dealing with things sensibly and realistically based on practical considerations
exampleSentence: We need a pragmatic approach to solve this problem.

definition: Open to more than one interpretation; having a double meaning
exampleSentence: The politician's statement was deliberately ambiguous.

definition: Not readily giving up; keeping a firm hold
exampleSentence: Her tenacious spirit helped her overcome every obstacle.

definition: Expressed clearly; easy to understand
exampleSentence: Despite being 90, she remained lucid and sharp-minded.

definition: Using more words than needed; long-winded
exampleSentence: His verbose email could have been summarized in two sentences.
etymology: From Latin 'verbosus' (full of words), from 'verbum' (word). The same root gives us 'verb' and 'proverb.'

definition: Truthful and straightforward; frank
exampleSentence: She was candid about the challenges ahead.

definition: Having an ability to accurately assess situations; shrewd
exampleSentence: The astute investor spotted the opportunity before anyone else.

definition: Well-meaning and kindly; generous and charitable
exampleSentence: The benevolent donor gave millions to local charities.

definition: To perceive or recognize something with difficulty
exampleSentence: It's hard to discern the truth from fiction in this case.

definition: Showing selfless concern for the wellbeing of others
exampleSentence: Her altruistic behavior inspired everyone around her.
etymology: Coined by philosopher Auguste Comte from Italian 'altrui' (of others) and Latin 'alter' (other). The deliberate opposite of 'egoistic.'

definition: A harsh, discordant mixture of sounds
exampleSentence: The construction site was a cacophony of drills and hammers.
etymology: From Greek 'kakophōnia,' combining 'kakos' (bad) + 'phōnē' (sound). The 'phōnē' root also lives in 'telephone' and 'symphony.'

definition: Having or showing care and effort in work or duties
exampleSentence: She was a diligent student who always completed her assignments.

definition: Difficult to interpret or understand; mysterious
exampleSentence: The Mona Lisa's enigmatic smile has puzzled art lovers for centuries.

definition: Happening by chance rather than intention; lucky
exampleSentence: Their meeting at the conference was entirely fortuitous.
etymology: From Latin 'fortuitus' (by chance), from 'fors' (luck). Originally it meant purely accidental — not necessarily positive.

definition: Fond of company; sociable
exampleSentence: He was a gregarious host who made everyone feel welcome.

definition: Excessive pride or self-confidence, often leading to downfall
exampleSentence: His hubris led him to underestimate his competition.
etymology: Directly from Greek 'hybris,' meaning violent arrogance against the gods. In Greek tragedy it was always the fatal flaw that led to downfall.

definition: Acting or done quickly without thought or care
exampleSentence: His impetuous decision to quit cost him dearly.

definition: Place or deal with close together for contrasting effect
exampleSentence: The artist juxtaposed dark and light colors to create tension.
etymology: From Latin 'juxta' (beside) + French 'poser' (to place). Literally: to set things side by side so their differences become visible.

definition: Relating to or resulting from motion; full of energy
exampleSentence: The performance had a kinetic energy that kept the audience on edge.

definition: Tending to talk a great deal; talkative
exampleSentence: The loquacious professor rarely finished a lecture on time.
etymology: From Latin 'loquax' (talkative), from 'loqui' (to speak). The same root gives us 'eloquent,' 'colloquial,' and 'soliloquy.'

definition: Make less severe, serious, or painful
exampleSentence: Wearing sunscreen can mitigate the risk of skin damage.

definition: Feeling or appearing casually calm and relaxed
exampleSentence: She seemed nonchalant about failing the exam.

definition: No longer produced or used; out of date
exampleSentence: Fax machines are becoming obsolete in the digital age.

definition: A seemingly absurd statement that when investigated proves to be true
exampleSentence: The paradox of choice suggests that more options can lead to less satisfaction.

definition: Complaining in a rather petulant or whining manner
exampleSentence: The querulous customer complained about every tiny detail.
etymology: From Latin 'querulus' (complaining), from 'queri' (to complain). Related to 'quarrel' and 'query' — all from a root about expressing discontent.

definition: Having an obstinately uncooperative attitude
exampleSentence: The recalcitrant employee refused to follow any instructions.
etymology: From Latin 'recalcitrare' (to kick back), from 'calx' (heel). It originally described a mule or horse that literally kicks backward against control.

definition: Enduring pain or hardship without showing feelings or complaining
exampleSentence: She remained stoic throughout the difficult medical procedure.

definition: Diverging from a topic; only marginally relevant
exampleSentence: His tangential comments derailed the entire meeting.
etymology: From Latin 'tangere' (to touch). A geometric tangent line merely 'touches' a curve without crossing — barely relevant, just touching the edge.

definition: Never done or known before; novel
exampleSentence: The pandemic caused unprecedented disruption to global economies.

definition: Having or showing a lack of thought or intelligence; mindless
exampleSentence: The interviewer was frustrated by his vacuous answers.
etymology: From Latin 'vacuus' (empty), from 'vacare' (to be empty). Related to 'vacuum,' 'vacant,' and 'vacation' — all share the idea of emptiness.

definition: Having a feeling of vague longing or regret
exampleSentence: She looked at old photographs with a wistful smile.

definition: Dislike or prejudice against people from other countries
exampleSentence: The rise of xenophobia is a concerning global trend.

definition: Having or showing great energy or enthusiasm in pursuit of a cause
exampleSentence: The zealous volunteer worked tirelessly for the community.

definition: Departing from an accepted standard; abnormal
exampleSentence: The scientist noted several aberrant results in the experiment.
etymology: From Latin 'aberrare' (to wander away), from 'ab-' (away) + 'errare' (to wander). Related to 'error' — both suggest straying from the right path.

definition: So lacking in originality as to be obvious and boring
exampleSentence: The film's banal plot failed to engage audiences.
etymology: From Old French 'banal' (belonging to a lord's public mill), meaning forced communal use. What everyone shared became synonymous with the ordinary.

definition: Kept secret or done secretively
exampleSentence: The spies held a clandestine meeting in the abandoned warehouse.
etymology: From Latin 'clandestinus' (hidden), from 'clam' (secretly). Shares a root with 'occult' — both describe things concealed from the public eye.

definition: A scarcity or lack of something
exampleSentence: There is a dearth of affordable housing in major cities.
etymology: From Old English 'deorþe' (dearness, costliness). What was once 'dear' (expensive) came to mean scarce — rare things always cost more.

definition: Having or showing great knowledge or learning
exampleSentence: The erudite professor could discuss any topic with authority.
etymology: From Latin 'eruditus' (polished, instructed), from 'e-' (out) + 'rudis' (rough). Education was seen as removing roughness — literally 'to de-rough.'

definition: A mistaken belief, especially one based on unsound arguments
exampleSentence: The idea that multitasking improves productivity is a common fallacy.

definition: Excessively talkative, especially on trivial matters
exampleSentence: The garrulous taxi driver didn't stop talking the entire journey.
etymology: From Latin 'garrulus' (chattering), from 'garrire' (to chatter). The root may be onomatopoeic — imitating the sound of unceasing birdsong or babbling.

definition: Intensely distressing; acutely painful
exampleSentence: The survivors told harrowing tales of the disaster.

definition: Never ending or always occurring; constant
exampleSentence: The incessant rain made the outdoor event miserable.

definition: Put something into a situation in which it could be harmed or lost
exampleSentence: His reckless behavior could jeopardize the entire project.

definition: Lose or lack vitality; grow weak
exampleSentence: The project languished for years without proper funding.
etymology: From Old French 'languiss-,' from Latin 'languere' (to be faint). Related to 'languid' and 'languor' — all evoke slow, drooping exhaustion.

definition: Friendly, good-natured, and easy to talk to
exampleSentence: The affable host made every guest feel immediately at ease.

definition: Reserved and saying little; not fond of talking
exampleSentence: The taciturn detective observed everything but said very little.
etymology: From Latin 'taciturnus' (silent), from 'tacere' (to be silent). The same root gives us 'tacit' — things understood without being spoken.

definition: Not revealing one's thoughts or feelings readily
exampleSentence: She was reticent about her personal life even with close friends.

definition: A person who acts obsequiously to gain favour; a flatterer
exampleSentence: The CEO was surrounded by sycophants who never questioned his decisions.
etymology: From Greek 'sykophantēs,' from 'sykon' (fig) + 'phainein' (to show). The exact origin is disputed — one theory involves a contemptuous fig gesture.

definition: The ability to understand and share the feelings of another
exampleSentence: Good leaders show empathy towards their team members.

definition: Affected by lethargy; sluggish and apathetic
exampleSentence: After the heavy meal, everyone felt lethargic and drowsy.

definition: Showing or having skill, especially with the hands
exampleSentence: The surgeon's dexterous fingers worked with remarkable precision.

definition: Tending to spend much time seated; involving little exercise
exampleSentence: A sedentary lifestyle can lead to various health problems.

definition: Strong, healthy, and full of energy
exampleSentence: She took a vigorous walk every morning to start her day.

definition: A proposed explanation made on the basis of limited evidence
exampleSentence: The scientist formulated a hypothesis before conducting experiments.

definition: Based on observation or experiment rather than theory
exampleSentence: The empirical evidence strongly supported their conclusion.
etymology: From Greek 'empeirikos' (experienced), from 'en-' (in) + 'peira' (trial). Knowledge built from direct experiment, not inherited from authority.

definition: A substance or person that causes or accelerates change
exampleSentence: The invention of the internet was a catalyst for global communication.

definition: A typical example or pattern; a model or framework
exampleSentence: The discovery caused a paradigm shift in how we understand the universe.
etymology: From Greek 'paradeigma' (pattern, example), from 'para-' (beside) + 'deiknynai' (to show). Thomas Kuhn gave it its modern scientific meaning in 1962.

definition: The combination of elements to form a connected whole
exampleSentence: The essay was a synthesis of ideas from multiple disciplines.

definition: A story or poem in which characters represent abstract ideas
exampleSentence: Animal Farm is a famous allegory about political corruption.

definition: The expression of meaning using language that normally signifies the opposite
exampleSentence: It was ironic that the fire station burned down.

definition: The art of effective or persuasive speaking or writing
exampleSentence: His speech was full of powerful rhetoric that inspired the crowd.

definition: A spoken or written account of connected events; a story
exampleSentence: The film's narrative kept audiences guessing until the final scene.

definition: Highly pleasing to the taste; delicious
exampleSentence: The chef prepared a delectable array of desserts.

definition: Having a pleasantly sharp taste or appetizing flavour
exampleSentence: The piquant sauce added a delightful kick to the dish.
etymology: From French 'piquant' (stinging), from 'piquer' (to prick). Related to 'pike' and 'peak' — all from a root about sharpness or a pointed end.

definition: Pleasantly salty or spicy, not sweet; appetizing
exampleSentence: She preferred savory snacks over sweet ones.

definition: Believing in or based on the principle of equality for all people
exampleSentence: The egalitarian society ensured equal opportunities for everyone.
etymology: From French 'égalitaire,' from Latin 'aequalis' (equal). The French Revolution's 'Liberté, égalité, fraternité' brought this concept into politics.

definition: A great difference or inequality between things
exampleSentence: The disparity in income between rich and poor continues to grow.

definition: The action of forming a unified whole; togetherness
exampleSentence: Team cohesion is essential for achieving shared goals.

definition: A system of government marked by excessive red tape and routine
exampleSentence: The startup moved fast to avoid becoming bogged down in bureaucracy.

definition: Anxious or fearful that something bad will happen
exampleSentence: She felt apprehensive before her first public speech.

definition: Characterized by a feeling of intense happiness and excitement
exampleSentence: The team was euphoric after winning the championship.

definition: Feeling or showing anger at what is perceived as unjust
exampleSentence: She was indignant at being accused of something she didn't do.

definition: A sentimental longing for the past, typically for a period or place with happy associations
exampleSentence: The old photos filled her with nostalgia for her childhood summers.

definition: Brisk and cheerful readiness to do something
exampleSentence: She accepted the challenge with great alacrity.
etymology: From Latin 'alacritas' (liveliness, eagerness), from 'alacer' (brisk). The root suggests energetic quickness — the opposite of sluggishness.

definition: A step-by-step procedure for solving a problem or accomplishing a task
exampleSentence: The algorithm sorted thousands of results in milliseconds.

definition: To repeat a process, making incremental improvements each time
exampleSentence: The team iterated on the design until it felt intuitive.

definition: An early model of a product used to test a concept before full development
exampleSentence: They built a prototype in two weeks to test user reactions.

definition: The delay between a request and the system's response
exampleSentence: High latency made the video call choppy and frustrating.
etymology: From Latin 'latens' (lying hidden), from 'latere' (to lie hidden). Related to 'latent' — something that exists but hasn't yet revealed itself.

definition: To convert data into a coded form to prevent unauthorized access
exampleSentence: All messages are encrypted end-to-end for privacy.

definition: Relating to mental processes such as thinking, knowing, and reasoning
exampleSentence: Regular reading improves cognitive function and memory.

definition: Belonging naturally; arising from internal motivation rather than external reward
exampleSentence: Her intrinsic love of learning drove her to study every day.
etymology: From Medieval Latin 'intrinsecus' (inward), from 'intra' (within). Describes a quality belonging to something by its very nature, not added from outside.

definition: A systematic inclination or prejudice that affects judgments unfairly
exampleSentence: Confirmation bias makes us seek information that supports existing beliefs.

definition: Something that causes a specific response or provokes action
exampleSentence: Light is a key stimulus that regulates our sleep cycle.

definition: The way in which something is interpreted and understood by the mind
exampleSentence: Our perception of time slows down in dangerous situations.

definition: The quality of being determined and not giving up despite difficulty
exampleSentence: Her tenacity in the face of failure inspired the whole team.

definition: To delay or postpone tasks, often unnecessarily
exampleSentence: Many students procrastinate on assignments until the night before they're due.

definition: To have a strong effect on someone; to feel meaningful or relevant
exampleSentence: The author's words resonated deeply with everyone who had experienced loss.

definition: To think carefully and at length about something
exampleSentence: She sat by the window to contemplate her next move in life.

definition: The quality of being honest and having strong moral principles
exampleSentence: She refused the bribe, protecting her integrity at any cost.

definition: Sparing in use of resources; economical and avoiding waste
exampleSentence: His frugal lifestyle allowed him to retire at forty.

definition: Generous in forgiving; showing a lofty and generous spirit
exampleSentence: The champion was magnanimous in victory, praising his opponent.
etymology: From Latin 'magnanimus' (great-souled), from 'magnus' (great) + 'animus' (soul). The 'magnus' root also gives us 'magnificent' and 'magnitude.'

definition: To examine or inspect closely and thoroughly
exampleSentence: The detective scrutinized every detail of the crime scene.

definition: To work jointly with others on a shared project or goal
exampleSentence: The two companies decided to collaborate on developing a groundbreaking product.

definition: Continued effort and determination despite difficulty or delay
exampleSentence: Perseverance through ten rejections finally earned him the role.

definition: To understand and share the feelings of another person
exampleSentence: A good therapist can empathize with clients without losing objectivity.

definition: Calm, peaceful, and untroubled; tranquil
exampleSentence: The lake at dawn was completely serene, without a ripple.

definition: Extremely happy and excited, often as a result of a success
exampleSentence: She was elated when she saw her name on the acceptance list.

definition: To have an intense longing or desire for something
exampleSentence: After years abroad, she yearned to return to her hometown.

definition: To continue working toward a goal despite difficulty or setbacks
exampleSentence: Despite multiple rejections, she persevered and finally got published.

definition: Unity and support among members of a group with common interests
exampleSentence: The workers showed solidarity by refusing to cross the picket line.

definition: Not excluding any group of people; welcoming diversity
exampleSentence: An inclusive workplace benefits from a wider range of perspectives.

definition: The desire to promote the welfare of others through generous donations of time or money
exampleSentence: His philanthropy funded hospitals and schools across the region.

definition: The state of being strong, active, and full of energy
exampleSentence: Daily exercise restored her vitality after months of fatigue.

definition: To express thoughts or feelings clearly and effectively in words
exampleSentence: He struggled to articulate exactly why the film had moved him so deeply.

definition: To make suffering, pain, or a problem less severe
exampleSentence: The medication helped alleviate her chronic back pain significantly.

definition: To wander slowly without a fixed route or purpose
exampleSentence: The river meandered lazily through the valley before reaching the sea.

definition: To develop or nurture a skill, relationship, or quality over time
exampleSentence: She spent years cultivating a network of trusted mentors in her industry.

definition: To become progressively worse in quality or condition
exampleSentence: The patient's health began to deteriorate rapidly in the final weeks.

definition: To go beyond ordinary limits; to surpass or rise above
exampleSentence: True art transcends cultural boundaries and speaks to all of humanity.
etymology: From Latin 'transcendere' (to climb over), from 'trans-' (across) + 'scandere' (to climb). 'Scandere' also gives us 'ascend,' 'descend,' and 'scandal.'

definition: To think about something carefully and at length
exampleSentence: She pondered the question for a long time before giving her answer.

definition: To stimulate or give rise to a reaction or feeling
exampleSentence: The controversial painting provoked heated debate among art critics.

definition: To voluntarily give up or surrender something
exampleSentence: The CEO reluctantly relinquished control of the company after the scandal.
etymology: From Latin 'relinquere' (to leave behind), from 're-' + 'linquere' (to leave). Related to 'relic' — objects left behind — and 'delinquent' — one who abandons duty.

definition: To introduce new methods, ideas, or products
exampleSentence: Companies that fail to innovate risk being overtaken by their competitors.

definition: To rise and fall irregularly; to vary unpredictably
exampleSentence: The stock prices fluctuated wildly throughout the trading day.

definition: With great care and attention to every detail
exampleSentence: The surgeon meticulously followed every step of the procedure.

definition: With passionate intensity and deep feeling
exampleSentence: She fervently believed that education was the key to changing the world.

definition: Without intention; accidentally
exampleSentence: He inadvertently revealed the surprise party when he mentioned the restaurant.
etymology: From Medieval Latin 'inadvertens,' from 'in-' (not) + 'advertere' (to turn toward). Related to 'advertise' — not turning attention toward something.

definition: With firm determination and unwavering purpose
exampleSentence: She resolutely refused to compromise on her core values.

definition: With hesitation or uncertainty; not definitively
exampleSentence: She tentatively raised her hand, unsure if her answer was correct.

definition: To a great or intense degree; deeply
exampleSentence: The documentary profoundly changed how he thought about climate change.

definition: Without stopping or yielding; persistently and without mercy
exampleSentence: The reporter relentlessly pursued the story despite numerous setbacks.

definition: With complete sincerity, enthusiasm, and commitment
exampleSentence: He wholeheartedly supported his partner's decision to change careers.

definition: Proceeding in a subtle and harmful way that is not easily noticed
exampleSentence: Misinformation spreads in an insidious way, slowly distorting public perception.
etymology: From Latin 'insidiosus' (cunning), from 'insidiae' (ambush), from 'insidere' (to sit in). Literally: danger lurking in ambush beneath an innocent surface.

definition: Having a friendly, pleasant, and good-natured manner
exampleSentence: The new neighbor was amiable and quickly became friends with everyone on the block.

definition: Designed to impress or attract notice; showy or pretentious
exampleSentence: His ostentatious mansion made the humble neighbors feel uncomfortable.
etymology: From Latin 'ostentare' (to show off), from 'ostendere' (to display). The root 'tendere' means to stretch — as if stretching something in front of others.

definition: Engaged in deep or serious thought, often with a hint of sadness
exampleSentence: She sat in a pensive mood, staring out at the rain-soaked street.

definition: Likely to change rapidly and unpredictably; easily aroused
exampleSentence: The volatile market made investors nervous about their portfolios.

definition: Producing a great deal of profit or financial gain
exampleSentence: Software engineering proved to be a highly lucrative career choice.

definition: Characterized by friendly goodwill and mutual agreement
exampleSentence: The former partners reached an amicable agreement and parted on good terms.

definition: Curious and eager to learn or know about things
exampleSentence: Children are naturally inquisitive, always asking questions about the world.

definition: A situation requiring a choice between two equally difficult options
exampleSentence: She faced a dilemma between pursuing her dream or staying close to family.

definition: A sudden, profound moment of realization or understanding
exampleSentence: While washing dishes, he had an epiphany that changed his entire career path.

definition: The force or speed of movement; growing strength of a trend or effort
exampleSentence: The campaign gained momentum after a celebrity shared the cause online.

definition: Difficult or challenging circumstances that test one's strength
exampleSentence: Great leaders are often defined by how they respond to adversity.

definition: A state of balance between opposing forces or elements
exampleSentence: After the disruption, the ecosystem gradually returned to equilibrium.
etymology: From Latin 'aequilibrium,' from 'aequus' (equal) + 'libra' (scales). 'Libra' is also the zodiac sign and the origin of the pound (lb) as a unit of weight.

definition: The state of being alone, often peacefully and by choice
exampleSentence: The writer valued solitude and retreated to a mountain cabin to finish his novel.

definition: The quality of being thankful and appreciative
exampleSentence: She expressed her gratitude by writing each person a heartfelt thank-you note.

definition: A mild or indirect expression used in place of an unpleasant one
exampleSentence: 'Letting go' is a common euphemism for firing an employee.
etymology: From Greek 'euphēmismos,' from 'eu-' (good) + 'phēmē' (speech). Literally 'good speaking' — using pleasant words to avoid unpleasant ones.

definition: A remarkable or observable fact, event, or circumstance
exampleSentence: The northern lights are a breathtaking natural phenomenon.

definition: A widely held but fixed and oversimplified image or idea of a group
exampleSentence: The film challenged the stereotype that scientists lack social skills.

definition: A compelling personal magnetism that inspires devotion or enthusiasm
exampleSentence: The young politician's charisma drew massive crowds wherever she spoke.

definition: The ability to recover quickly from difficulties or bounce back
exampleSentence: The community showed remarkable resilience in rebuilding after the flood.

definition: The right to self-governance or freedom to make one's own decisions
exampleSentence: Remote workers often cite autonomy as the biggest advantage of their work style.

definition: The state of having mixed or contradictory feelings about something
exampleSentence: She felt ambivalence about moving abroad — excited by opportunity but sad to leave friends.
etymology: Coined by psychiatrist Eugen Bleuler (~1910) from Latin 'ambi-' (both) + 'valentia' (strength). Originally a clinical term for holding two contradictory feelings at once.
